MLS Commissioner Don Garber has previously stated his desire for MLS to be one of the top leagues in the world by 2022. To do so, the United States must adopt a promotion relegation system that is in use in every major soccer league in the world. The promotion relegation system ensures the highest level of competition in our domestic leagues, allowing our youth to develop to compete amongst the world’s elite. In a recent poll, 64% of polled MLS players were in favor of a promotion relegation system.

That furthers our national team. Something is at stake week in, week out. Be it at the top or at the bottom, you always have to perform. This thrill of the relegation battle is non-existent in the U.S. league –Jürgen Klinsmann

But, this post’s intention is not to argue why promotion relegation is needed, but rather to suggest a system that could work.

The first step to creating a football pyramid that contends with the likes of Germany and England is to have two top divisions. Since its inception, MLS has strived to create a sustainable top tier soccer league. Twenty years later, it’s still growing at a rapid rate and its popularity has caused smaller lower level leagues such as the NASL, Division II, and USL, Division III, to form. However, at this time, neither league is large enough or strong enough to be a standalone MLS II. By 2018, MLS will look something like this:

After a few years of stabilization, allowing the new franchises to solidify themselves, MLS should create MLS II. Now there are two ways I can see this occurring, either combining the NASL and USL, excluding the MLS reserve teams, or creating a wholly new league that allows teams from either division to join. MLS and MLS II would be a single entity with combined TV rights and revenue sharing. MLS II would model MLS, twenty-four teams, two conferences, East and West. At this point, a full promotion relegation pyramid would be too ambitious and would create backlash from owners concerned with losing their return on investment. Creating a two division promotion system essentially creates a floor for these teams that reduces the risk associated with a true promotion relegations system while also sharing profits across the whole system without too much dilution.

As for how the promotion relegation system would work, each year the bottom team in each conference from MLS would be automatically relegated to MLS II and the top team from each conference in MLS II would be automatically promoted to MLS. The 11th placed teams from each MLS conference would play a two legged playoff (a la Germany) against the 2nd placed teams from their respective MLS II Conferences, with the second leg being a home match for the MLS team.
